title: Astronomy
summary: Explore the universe: the Earth, Moon and sky, the solar system and distances, gravity and orbits with Kepler's laws, stars and light-years, galaxies and the expanding universe, and telescopes and astronomy in Africa.
audience: Students, teachers, stargazers and anyone curious about the universe

body.p: Astronomy is the oldest science. People everywhere have watched the sky to keep time, plan farming and navigate; many African cultures have rich star knowledge, such as using the rising of the Pleiades to mark planting seasons.

list: A day is one rotation of the Earth on its axis; the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west.
A year is one orbit of the Sun, about 365.25 days, which is why leap years add a day every four years.
Seasons happen because the Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.5°, so each hemisphere receives more direct sunlight for part of the year. They are not caused by changing distance from the Sun.
Near the equator, day length changes little through the year, and seasons are often marked more by rainfall than temperature.

body.p: The Moon orbits the Earth about every 27.3 days, but its cycle of phases (new moon, crescent, quarter, gibbous, full) takes about 29.5 days. Phases come from how much of the sunlit half we see. A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth; a lunar eclipse when the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

body.tip: Watch the Moon at the same time on several evenings and sketch its shape; you will see the phase cycle for yourself.

body.p: The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust. The Sun contains over 99% of its mass.

list: Inner rocky planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
Outer giant planets: Jupiter and Saturn (gas giants), Uranus and Neptune (ice giants).
Dwarf planets such as Pluto and Ceres, plus asteroids, comets and moons.
A memory aid for the order: "My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming".

body.p: The average Earth-Sun distance, about 150 million km, is called one astronomical unit (AU). Light travelling at 3 x 10⁸ m/s takes about 1.496 x 10¹¹ / 3 x 10⁸, roughly 499 seconds or 8.3 minutes, to reach us, so we always see the Sun as it was about eight minutes ago.

body.tip: Make a scale model: if the Sun is a football, the Earth is a peppercorn about 25 metres away. Space is mostly empty.

body.p: Gravity is the attraction between masses. It holds the Moon in orbit around Earth and the planets around the Sun. Newton showed that the same force that makes a mango fall also keeps the Moon in orbit: the Moon is constantly falling towards Earth while moving sideways fast enough to keep missing it.

list: Planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus.
A planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun.

The square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of its average distance. Measuring the period T in years and distance a in AU, T² = a³. Mars, at about 1.52 AU, takes about 1.52^1.5 = 1.87 years to orbit; Jupiter, at about 5.2 AU, takes about 11.9 years.

body.p: Artificial satellites provide communication, weather forecasting, navigation (GPS) and Earth observation used for farming and disaster response. Several African countries, including Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt, Kenya, Ghana and Rwanda, have launched satellites.

body.tip: Use T² = a³ to check any planet's orbital period from its distance in AU.

body.p: Stars are huge balls of hot gas, mostly hydrogen and helium, powered by nuclear fusion in their cores, where hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium and release energy.

A light-year is the distance light travels in a year: about 3 x 10⁵ km/s x 365.25 x 86 400 s, roughly 9.46 x 10¹² km. The nearest star beyond the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.24 light-years away, about 4.0 x 10¹³ km. Looking at distant stars means looking back in time.

list: Stars form in clouds of gas and dust called nebulae.
Most of a star's life is spent fusing hydrogen (the main sequence).
Stars like the Sun swell into red giants and end as white dwarfs.
Much more massive stars explode as supernovae, leaving neutron stars or black holes, and scatter elements such as carbon, oxygen and iron into space; the atoms in your body were made in stars.

body.p: Spectroscopy splits starlight into colours; dark lines reveal a star's composition, temperature and motion.

body.tip: A star's colour indicates its temperature: blue stars are hottest, red stars coolest.

body.p: Our Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way galaxy, a barred spiral about 100 000 light-years across. The Milky Way is one of hundreds of billions of galaxies in the observable universe.

Edwin Hubble found that distant galaxies are moving away from us, faster the further away they are: v = H₀d. With a Hubble constant of about 70 km/s per megaparsec, a galaxy 100 megaparsecs away recedes at about 70 x 100 = 7000 km/s. Running the expansion backwards leads to the Big Bang, about 13.8 billion years ago, supported by evidence such as the cosmic microwave background radiation.

list: Dark matter: unseen mass that holds galaxies together.
Dark energy: whatever is accelerating the expansion of the universe.
Exoplanets: thousands of planets orbit other stars; are any home to life?

body.tip: Find the Milky Way on a dark, moonless night away from city lights; it looks like a faint band of cloud across the sky.

body.p: Telescopes gather light (or other radiation) to see faint and distant objects. Optical telescopes use lenses or mirrors; radio telescopes detect radio waves; space telescopes avoid the blurring and absorption of Earth's atmosphere.

list: The Southern African Large Telescope (SALT) in Sutherland, South Africa, is one of the largest single optical telescopes in the southern hemisphere.
MeerKAT, a radio telescope of 64 dishes in the Karoo, has produced striking images of the centre of the Milky Way.
The Square Kilometre Array (SKA), being built in South Africa and Australia, with partner sites in other African countries, will be one of the world's largest scientific facilities.
Africa's dark skies, such as in Namibia, attract astronomers and astro-tourism.
Traditional astronomy: many African cultures named stars, used them for calendars and told stories about them.

body.p: Astronomy careers include research, engineering, data science and software, and science communication. Free planetarium apps let anyone identify stars and planets.

body.tip: Join a local astronomy club or star party; many hold free public viewing nights.
